job.style: a market or shop situation that uses the idea

passage: Rohan visited a packaging factory to see how boxes are made for shipping goods. The manager showed him a flat cardboard sheet cut into a specific pattern, known as a net, which folds perfectly into a cube. Rohan noticed that a cylinder's net is different; it consists of two circular bases and a rectangular sheet whose length must exactly match the circumference of the circles to fit perfectly. The manager explained that a triangular prism has five faces: two triangular ends and three rectangular sides. He also pointed out a cone, noting that its curved surface meets at a single point called the apex or vertex. Finally, they looked at a solid block where the manager used Euler's formula, F + V - E = 2, to verify the count of faces, vertices, and edges. He reminded Rohan that a cylinder has two curved edges where the flat circular faces meet the curved surface, proving that edges can exist on round objects.

items.evidence: Rohan noticed that a cylinder's net is different; it consists of two circular bases and a rectangular sheet whose length must exactly match the circumference of the circles to fit perfectly.
items.q: A worker cuts a cylinder net's rectangle shorter than the circles' circumference. What happens?
options: The sheet cannot wrap fully around the circles
The sheet still fits, as any length works
The sheet fits if the circles are made larger
The sheet fits if one circle is left out
items.explain: The rectangle's length must exactly match the circles' circumference, so a shorter sheet cannot close.

wrong.why: thinks the rectangle can be any length
reverses the size link; bigger circles need a longer sheet
misreads the net as needing only one base

items.evidence: The manager explained that a triangular prism has five faces: two triangular ends and three rectangular sides.
items.q: A chocolate box is a triangular prism. How many flat pieces make up its faces?
options: Five: two triangles and three rectangles
Three: one for each side of the triangle
Four: only the faces you can see
items.explain: A triangular prism has two triangular ends and three rectangular sides, making five faces.

wrong.why: counts faces from the triangle's sides
counts only faces visible in a picture

items.evidence: He also pointed out a cone, noting that its curved surface meets at a single point called the apex or vertex.
items.q: Priya says a cone has no vertex because its top is curved. Which fact shows she is wrong?
options: Its curved surface comes together at one tip
Its curved surface has a vertex everywhere
Its curved surface counts as a flat face
Its curved surface has a straight edge
items.explain: A cone's curved surface meets at a single point, the apex, which is its vertex.

wrong.why: thinks any point on a solid is a vertex
thinks edges are straight lines drawn on solids

items.evidence: He reminded Rohan that a cylinder has two curved edges where the flat circular faces meet the curved surface, proving that edges can exist on round objects.
items.q: Amit thinks round objects cannot have edges. How many edges does a cylinder really have?
options: Two, where the circles meet the curved side
None, because a cylinder is round
Three, one for each of its surfaces
One, the straight line down its side
items.explain: A cylinder has two curved edges where its flat circular faces meet the curved surface.

wrong.why: thinks round solids have no edges
thinks only straight lines count as edges
